title: Linguistic analysis (Cantonese)
content_html:
Linguistic analysis (Cantonese)

Note: Yale or Jyutping romanization: Yale and Jyutping are two systems for writing Cantonese sounds with the Latin alphabet. Yale (Cantonese) was developed at Yale in the 1950s for learners. It shows tones with diacritics (macron, acute, grave) and adds a trailing h to mark low‐register tones (e.g., sī/sí/si; sìh/síh/sih).

Example: 廣東話 → Gwóngdūng wá.

Jyutping was created by the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong (1993). It marks tones with numbers 1–6 (e.g., si1/si2/si3/si4/si5/si6) and uses distinctive spellings: z/c for [ts]/[tsʰ], j for the glide [j], and finals like eo/oe.

Example: 廣東話 → gwong2 dung1 waa2.

100 words each followed by Cantonese as a 10x10 grid

Here are concrete directions for deeper analysis

reflection_lexicon_linguistic_analysis.html

What you can analyze further

  • Map semantic fields (optics, perception, memory, meta) and tighten group labels.
  • Build a network of lexical relations: synonymy/antonymy (e.g., clarity ↔ opacity), hypernyms (e.g., memory ⊃ episodic/semantic).
  • Polysemy inventory: e.g., reflection = optical image vs. introspection; classify senses and attach examples.
  • Translation strategies: direct vs. idiomatic vs. technical terms (e.g. 記憶術).
  • Literal–idiomatic divergence: use your “literal gloss” column to quantify how far each item is from a word-for-word mapping.
  • Part-of-speech alignment: English nouns vs. Cantonese noun/verb/adjective realizations.
  • Compound patterns: prefixes/suffixes and morphemes (e.g. 記 憶 再 自我 術).
  • Character productivity: which characters function as productive morphemes in this set (e.g. 記 憶 光 影 證
  • Affix-like behaviour: quantify pseudo-affixes (e.g. 術) and semantic roles.
  • Tone distribution: which tones dominate? Are memory-cluster terms skewed to certain tones?
  • Syllable structure: counts (done), coda distribution (-n/-ng/-p/-t/-k/Ø), onsets (z/c/j…).
  • Homophony: cluster by identical Jyutping strings; check where homophones map to different meanings.
  • Radicals and semantic hints: group by radicals (e.g. 言 心 光 見) and correlate with semantic fields.
  • Character frequency (done): extend to bigram/trigram frequencies at the character level.
  • Align each word to frames: Seeing → Attending → Remembering → Retrieving → Evaluating → Meta.
  • Build a script (event sequence) and test alternative orderings; compute path coherence scores (e.g., minimal cross-frame jumps).
  • Tag metaphor mappings (e.g., SEEING → KNOWING, KNOWLEDGE → CLARITY) and count which items instantiate them.
  • Use the Source–Path–Goal schema to justify the overall progression.
  • Collocation profiles: for each English item, extract top collocates; compare to Chinese collocates for the translation.
  • Distributional semantics: embed the English list with word vectors, cluster, and compare to a character- or word-level embedding of the Chinese items.
  • Concreteness/AoA (Age of Acquisition) ratings for English; inspect whether “optics” terms are more concrete than “meta” terms.
  • Valence/arousal: map affective norms (e.g., nostalgia vs. evidence).
  • Memory architecture mapping: align encoding→storage→retrieval terms to standard models; check completeness.
  • Build minimal pairs (clarity–opacity; reflection–refraction).
  • Create spaced-repetition decks using your phases as interleaved strands.
  • Add romanization practice: tone-pair drills for items with similar segments across tones.

Group the 100 words by the subset

[grouping_by_subset.html]

Notes:

  • Each item appears in exactly one bucket (no overlaps), using your subset as the top-level categories.
  • “Reflection and memory” collects the core memory architecture and repositories (schema/index/archive…).
  • “Ripple” covers wave/echo/dynamic effects (echo, afterimage, glint/glimmer/shimmer, bloom, feedback/loop/recursion).
  • “Mirror surface” handles static image structure (mirror, surface, depth, inversion, symmetry, double, doppelgänger, shadow, silhouette, appearance).
  • “Illusion” focuses on appearance quality/physics (illusion, refraction, clarity, transparency, opacity).
  • “Observer” is apparatus/viewpoint (observer, lens, perspective, screen, frame, filter).
  • “Awareness” is metacognitive/phenomenological states (awareness, mindfulness… meditation, imagination/projection/fantasy/dream).
  • “Recollection” captures access/experiences (retrieval, cue, priming, recollection/recall/recognition/familiarity/déjà vu, witness/testimony/evidence).
  • “Distortion” currently holds the single item distortion. If you prefer, I can fold it into “Illusion” or “Ripple.”
  • “Wisdom” culminates the pathway (insight, wisdom, understanding).

I’ve allowed overlaps and folded Distortion → Illusion (kept as an alias so you can still filter by it). You’ll see per-item group memberships, group counts, and full listings.
